rationale: Active export-control regime on exactly this bill of materials' inputs: gallium/germanium licensing since Aug 2023; a United States-specific export ban (Dec 2024) suspended only until 27 Nov 2026; licensing on seven medium/heavy rare earths since Apr 2025 (still in force); Oct 2025 package covering more rare earths, lithium batteries and graphite anode material suspended only until 10 Nov 2026; ban on dual-use exports to United States military end users remains in force. Also a covered foreign country under FY2020 National Defense Authorization Act section 848 for drone critical components. Not 1.0 because commercial licences are still being granted.
Comprehensive United States sanctions; not a viable source for a defense program.

Holds about two-thirds of advanced chip capacity (TrendForce 2024), so a single shock has no fallback. Low day-to-day disruption risk, but a cross-strait blockade or conflict is a severe tail risk. Scored well below China because there is no export-control regime targeting United States buyers.
Treaty ally; reliable supplier. Some regional (North Korea) tail risk.
Treaty ally. Main exposure is natural disasters (earthquakes have halted chip and materials plants before).
Friendly; scored up for transshipment risk (re-export of Chinese-origin goods complicates traceability).
Free-trade partner under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement and near-shore; scored for border, tariff-policy and logistics variability.
North Atlantic Treaty Organization ally; stable.
Stable; neutral but reliable trade partner.
Domestic. Not zero: single plants still have fires; strikes and capacity limits.
Ally; integrated into the United States defense industrial base.
Policy risk (state role in lithium; royalty changes).
Friendly; moderate policy and logistics risk.
Fragmented or unknown origin. Deliberately conservative: unknown provenance is itself a risk.
